etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English chaunten, from Old French chanter, from Latin cantāre (“sing”). Doublet of cant.

definitions.definition: To sing, especially without instruments, and as applied to monophonic and pre-modern music.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto VII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 3:
quote.text: the cherefull birds of sundry kind / Do chaunt sweet musick, to delight his mind

definitions.definition: To sing or intone sacred text.
To utter or repeat in a strongly rhythmical manner, especially as a group.

quote.citation: 2009, Leo J. Daugherty III, The Marine Corps and the State Department, page 116:
quote.text: On their way to Parliament Square, the demonstrators chanted slogans, sang the Hungarian national anthem, and waved banners and Hungarian flags (minus the hated Communist emblem).

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To sell horses fraudulently, exaggerating their merits.
Type of singing done generally without instruments and harmony.

(music, Anglicanism) A harmonized melody used in Anglican chant, usually split into two two-bar phrases, to which the words of a psalm are sung by a choir; typically, each musical phrase corresponds to the text of half of a verse.
(music) A short and simple melody to which unmetrical psalms, etc., are sung or recited.
Twang; manner of speaking; a canting tone.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter XVII, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: His strange face, his strange chant.

definitions.definition: A repetitive song, typically an incantation or part of a ritual.
